title: Dark-Roux Shrimp & Crab Gumbo with Steamed Rice
dek: A patient mahogany roux, shrimp-shell stock, tender okra and the Cajun trinity build a deeply savory gumbo finished with pearly shrimp, sweet lump crab and a mound of white rice.
image_alt: Shrimp and crab gumbo in a dark roux broth beside a mound of white rice, finished with parsley
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb large shell-on shrimp, 21 to 25 count, thawed if frozen
8 oz refrigerated pasteurized lump crab meat, picked over for shell
2 cups long-grain white rice, rinsed until the water is mostly clear
2 1/4 tsp Diamond Crystal kosher salt, divided, plus more to taste
3/4 cup neutral oil, such as avocado or canola
1 large yellow onion, cut into 1/4-inch dice (about 2 cups)
1 large green bell pepper, cut into 1/4-inch dice (about 1 1/2 cups)
3 celery ribs, cut into 1/4-inch dice (about 1 cup)
1/2 tsp cayenne pepper, plus more to taste
10 oz frozen sliced okra, thawed and patted very dry
4 scallions, thinly sliced, white and green parts separated

instructions.name: Peel the shrimp and make a shell stock
instructions.text: Peel and devein the shrimp, reserving every shell. Refrigerate the shrimp. Combine the shells, 7 cups cold water, 1 bay leaf and the peppercorns in a saucepan. Bring just to a boil, reduce to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered for 25 minutes. Strain through a fine-mesh sieve without pressing the shells; measure 6 cups stock, adding water only if needed. Keep hot over low heat.

instructions.name: Steam the rice separately
instructions.text: Combine the rinsed rice, 3 cups water and 3/4 teaspoon salt in a medium saucepan. Bring to a boil, stir once, cover and reduce to the lowest heat. Cook 16 minutes, remove from the heat and rest covered for 10 minutes. Fluff, cover again and hold off heat so the grains stay distinct for the photographed rice mounds.

instructions.name: Cook the roux to mahogany
instructions.text: Heat the oil in a heavy 6-quart Dutch oven over medium. Add the flour and whisk until smooth. Cook 28 to 35 minutes, switching to a flat-ended wooden spoon once the mixture loosens, and stir constantly into every corner until the roux is the color of milk chocolate. Lower the heat if it smokes or dark specks appear. If it smells scorched, discard it and begin again; burned roux cannot be repaired.

instructions.name: Stop the roux with the Cajun trinity
instructions.text: Immediately add the onion, bell pepper and celery; the vegetables will hiss and cool the roux. Cook over medium-low heat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring frequently, until softened. Add the garlic, tomato paste, paprika, thyme, cayenne, black pepper, scallion whites and remaining bay leaf. Cook 2 minutes until fragrant and the tomato paste darkens.

instructions.name: Sear away the okra's excess moisture
instructions.text: While the trinity softens, heat a dry 12-inch skillet over medium-high. Add the well-dried okra and cook 6 to 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the surfaces lose their frosty wetness and several edges brown. Scrape the okra into the Dutch oven. This separate step keeps the gumbo cohesive rather than stringy.

instructions.name: Whisk in stock and simmer slowly
instructions.text: Add the hot shrimp stock to the roux mixture 1 cup at a time, whisking smooth after each addition. Stir in the Worcestershire and 1 1/4 teaspoons salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a steady uncovered simmer for 40 to 45 minutes. Stir along the bottom every 8 to 10 minutes and skim only obvious pools of oil; the finished broth should coat a spoon lightly but remain ladleable.

instructions.name: Poach the shrimp and fold in the crab safely
instructions.text: Season the chilled shrimp with the remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt. Add them to the gently simmering gumbo and cook 3 to 5 minutes, stirring once, until their flesh is firm, pearly and opaque; the thickest shrimp should reach 145°F when checked with a thin-probe thermometer. Fold in the crab and heat 1 to 2 minutes, just until steaming, so the lumps stay intact.

instructions.name: Brighten and plate like the photograph
instructions.text: Remove both bay leaves. Stir in the lemon juice, half the scallion greens and half the parsley. Taste and adjust salt, cayenne or hot sauce. Pack about 3/4 cup rice into a small bowl and invert it into each wide shallow bowl. Ladle the dark gumbo around—not over—the rice, position visible shrimp and crab near the front, and finish with the remaining parsley and scallions plus a few drops of hot sauce on the rice if desired.

why_it_works: Shrimp shells make a focused stock in 25 minutes, giving the gumbo a seafood backbone without requiring bottled clam juice or an all-day broth.
Cooking equal volumes of oil and flour to milk-chocolate brown creates roasted depth; adding the trinity immediately arrests the browning before the roux burns.
Dry-searing thawed okra evaporates surface water and reduces stringiness before it joins the long-simmered broth.
Adding shrimp only after the gumbo base is finished prevents the long simmer from turning them tight and rubbery, while pasteurized crab needs only gentle reheating.
Rice cooked in a separate covered pan remains fluffy and gives each bowl the distinct white mound surrounded by dark seafood broth shown in the finished photograph.
swaps: Replace the lump crab with 12 ounces of firm white fish cut into 1-inch pieces. Add it 2 minutes before the shrimp and cook until both reach 145°F and the fish flakes easily.
For shrimp-only gumbo, increase the shell-on shrimp to 2 pounds and omit the crab; use the extra shells in the stock and divide the peeled shrimp evenly among eight bowls.
Fresh okra can replace frozen: slice 12 ounces into 1/2-inch rounds and dry-sear for 8 to 10 minutes until lightly browned.
Use a good-quality low-sodium seafood stock when shell-on shrimp are unavailable. Start with 6 cups and skip the stock-making step, but do not substitute strongly salted bouillon.
Brown rice can replace white rice, but cook it according to its package timing and start it before the roux so it is ready when the seafood goes into the pot.
storage: Cool the gumbo and rice in separate shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours. Keep the gumbo up to 3 days and the rice up to 4 days. Reheat gumbo gently over medium-low heat, stirring often, until it reaches 165°F; microwave rice with 1 tablespoon water per cup until 165°F. For best freezer texture, freeze the finished roux-and-okra base before adding seafood for up to 3 months, thaw overnight, bring to a simmer and add fresh shrimp and crab. Fully cooked gumbo can be frozen up to 2 months, but the shrimp will be firmer after reheating.
notes: A heavy, light-colored Dutch oven makes the roux's color easier to judge than a black interior. Stir continuously and keep the trinity measured before the flour touches the oil.
Milk-chocolate brown is dark enough for roasted flavor while retaining practical thickening power. Taking the roux nearly black is riskier and makes a thinner broth.
Refrigerated pasteurized lump crab is already cooked. Pick it over gently with your fingertips for shell fragments and fold it in at the end rather than simmering it apart.
Do not boil filé powder in the pot because it can turn ropey. If you enjoy sassafras filé, offer it at the table for diners to stir into individual bowls.
Calories and cost are estimates per serving, including rice. Crab price, shrimp size and the amount of cooking oil retained in the broth cause the largest variation.

faqs.q: How is this gumbo different from shrimp étouffée?
faqs.a: This gumbo uses an oil-based roux cooked much darker, six cups of shrimp-shell stock, okra and a longer simmer to make a ladleable stew. Étouffée is usually a smaller batch of shrimp in a lighter, butter-rich gravy spooned around rice. The ingredients overlap, but the roux color, liquid ratio and finished texture are different.

faqs.q: Can I make the gumbo base a day ahead?
faqs.a: Yes. Complete the recipe through the 45-minute simmer, cool the base in shallow containers and refrigerate up to 2 days. Reheat it to a steady simmer, then add the raw shrimp and cooked crab as directed. Cook fresh rice while the base reheats.

faqs.q: What should I do if my roux looks separated or lumpy?
faqs.a: A glossy layer of oil can appear as a dark roux cooks and is not automatically a failure; keep stirring and add the vegetables on schedule. After the vegetables soften, whisk hot stock in gradually. Hard black flecks or an acrid smell indicate scorching, and the only reliable fix is to discard the roux and restart.
